title: The Western Myth of Russian Greatness
gist: Christian Caryl argues that a centuries-long Western habit of projecting fantasies onto Russia — from Voltaire through Duranty and the 2009 Medvedev reset to today's MAGA influencers — has systematically inflated estimates of Russian power, and that this error has warped professional analysis: Gen. Mark Milley told Biden Kyiv could fall in 72 hours, Mearsheimer kept predicting Ukraine's imminent demise, and Samuel Charap called the war unwinnable. He also flags the Economist's 10,000 words of coverage for sanctioned billionaire Andrey Melnichenko as an effective Kremlin rehabilitation play.

insights.claim: A long list of military experts, academics, think-tankers and journalists have had their analyses of the Ukraine war warped by overestimating Russian capacities, making the U.S. policy elite structurally prone to misreading Russia.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Treat consensus Russia-strength forecasts as biased high; the same bias likely infects commodity, defense and Eastern European risk pricing.
insights.quote: the U.S. policy elite has long seemed to have a particular weakness for misreading Russia—from Cold War-era Sovietologists to U.S. President Donald Trump

insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: A documented, catastrophic miss from the top of the U.S. military establishment — a calibration benchmark for discounting official threat assessments.

insights.so_what: Named-analyst track records are a usable filter: realists systematically over-weighted Russian material superiority over institutional quality.

insights.claim: The Economist devoted a 7,000-word profile by its Moscow correspondent plus a 3,000-word essay by the subject himself to heavily sanctioned Russian billionaire Andrey Melnichenko, depicting him as a prominent voice of reform.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Elite Western media legitimizing sanctioned oligarchs is a leading indicator of a sanctions-relief lobbying cycle — watch for delisting campaigns.

insights.claim: Melnichenko's essay was vague on specific demands for internal Russian change but expansive in demanding recognition of Russia's great-power status, and said nothing Putin himself could not have said.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: A test to apply to any 'reformist oligarch' pitch: reform demands must be specific and domestic, or it is status-seeking cover.

insights.claim: An oligarch of Melnichenko's stature would be highly unlikely to publish such a document in a Western publication without tacit Kremlin acceptance, making the Economist's coverage a more effective boost to Russia's global rehabilitation than the Kremlin's American or European far-right allies could manage.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Mainstream-outlet channels, not fringe media, are where sanctions-rehabilitation narratives get real traction — monitor them as a policy leading indicator.
insights.quote: The Economist has boosted the case for Russia’s global rehabilitation far more effectively than the Kremlin’s friends on the American or European far right could have done.

insights.claim: Melnichenko's essay inveighed against unfair Western rules while never mentioning that the Kremlin is party to numerous international and bilateral agreements it has violated, several of which recognize Ukraine's sovereignty and borders.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Treaty-violation history is the argument that defeats grievance-based sanctions-relief cases; useful for handicapping relief odds.

themes.theme: Russian domestic weakness the boosters miss

insights.claim: Russians spend a far higher share of their incomes on food than Western Europeans, have extremely high divorce rates, and face an epidemic of domestic violence, aided by a law passed a few years ago decriminalizing wife-beating.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Household-level distress metrics undercut the traditional-values marketing and point to a weaker consumer economy than headline GDP implies.
insights.locator: Tucker Carlson (of testicle-tanning fame)

insights.claim: The fantasists of Russian power repeatedly miss the country's obvious signs of weakness, underdevelopment, corruption and societal decay, partly because Russia boosters rarely travel beyond big cities or meet ordinary people.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: A concrete research heuristic: discount Russia assessments built only on Moscow and St. Petersburg observation.
insights.quote: Again and again, the fantasists of Russian power miss the country’s obvious signs of weakness, underdevelopment, corruption, and societal decay.

themes.theme: Kremlin influence operations and Western amplifiers

insights.claim: In 2024 U.S. prosecutors indicted two Russian agents for funneling money to conservative influencers who circulated pro-Putin views on their social media platforms, evidence that figures like Candace Owens and Tucker Carlson have been highly effective amplifiers of Russian narratives.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Paid-influence indictments are a documented channel; treat pro-Moscow narrative surges in U.S. media as potentially sponsored rather than organic.

themes.theme: A three-century pattern of Russophile self-deception

insights.claim: For centuries Russian rulers have exploited Westerners' overactive imaginations, going back to Voltaire — who praised Catherine the Great and applauded her most brutal conquests while never actually visiting, and whose long-distance propaganda Catherine was happy to subsidize.
insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
insights.so_what: Establishes the base rate: Western enthusiasm for Russia is a recurring, sponsored phenomenon, not new information about Russia.

insights.so_what: Historic precedent for prominent Western observers endorsing Russian governance at the exact moment it was most repressive.

insights.speaker: Christian Caryl
